name: Erevos Maw

stars.name: Erevos
stars.notes: Stellar-mass black hole with a thin accretion disk fed by captured interstellar medium. Event horizon radius approximately 24 km. Accretion disk emits in x-ray and visible spectra, providing the system's only illumination. No companion star—Erevos feeds on passing gas and dust.

anomalies.name: The Accretion Whisper
anomalies.notes: The accretion disk's x-ray emissions contain quasi-periodic oscillations at 43.7 Hz that carry what appears to be structured information. Analysis suggests the modulation is not natural—the pattern complexity exceeds what accretion physics can produce. Source and meaning unknown.

anomalies.name: The Lensed Archive
anomalies.location: Light cone behind Erevos relative to galactic core
anomalies.notes: Erevos's gravitational lensing amplifies and distorts light from objects behind it. Within this lensed field, observers have detected what appear to be artificial structures at extreme distances—megastructures in other star systems, visible only through Erevos's magnification. Whether these structures still exist or are light-echoes from the distant past is unknown.

asteroid_belts.name: The Offering
asteroid_belts.location: Diffuse ring at 0.8 AU, slowly spiraling inward
asteroid_belts.notes: Captured debris slowly accreting toward the black hole. Includes anomalous metallic fragments with regular geometry—possibly remnants of artificial objects that strayed too close. Transit time from current position to the event horizon is estimated at 40,000 years.

stations.name: Event Horizon Observatory
stations.location: Stable orbit at 8.4 AU from Erevos
stations.notes: Joint research facility operated by the Gravitational Physics Consortium and the Anomaly Studies Division. Primary missions: accretion disk physics, gravitational lensing observation, and analysis of the Accretion Whisper's modulated emissions. Heavily shielded against x-ray flux.

faction_control.notes: The Consortium holds the primary research charter. The Anomaly Studies Division maintains a secondary presence focused on the Accretion Whisper and the Lensed Archive. Military patrols occasionally transit the area to verify no unauthorized approach to the black hole.

history: Erevos was detected in 2278 via its x-ray emissions and confirmed as a stellar-mass black hole through radial velocity measurements of nearby stars. Initial classification was routine—one of thousands of known stellar-mass black holes.

The Event Horizon Observatory was established in 2401 to study accretion disk physics. In 2423, researchers analyzing x-ray data discovered the structured modulation now called the Accretion Whisper. The finding remains controversial—some physicists argue the pattern is a statistical artifact, while others insist its complexity exceeds natural processes by orders of magnitude.

The Lensed Archive was discovered in 2456 when observers using Erevos as a gravitational lens detected what appeared to be megastructures in distant systems. If real, these are the first evidence of large-scale engineering by non-human intelligence observed at interstellar distances. Verification efforts continue.
description: Erevos Maw is a wound in spacetime—eight solar masses compressed into a sphere smaller than a city, wrapped in a thin disk of superheated matter spiraling toward oblivion. The black hole offers no planets, no surfaces, no ground to stand on. What it offers instead is a lens, a laboratory, and a mystery. The accretion disk glows with the blue-white fury of matter being torn apart at the atomic level, and within that fury, something is whispering in structured x-rays that should not carry information but apparently do.

The Erevos Maw's scientific value lies in two discoveries that have not been fully accepted by the broader research community. The Accretion Whisper—modulated x-ray emissions with information-like structure—challenges the assumption that accretion disks are purely thermodynamic systems. The Lensed Archive—apparent megastructures visible through gravitational magnification—challenges the assumption that humanity is alone in building on astronomical scales. Both discoveries tread the uncomfortable border between observation and interpretation, and both refuse to resolve into certainty.

Twenty-two researchers live at the Event Horizon Observatory, studying a black hole that may be talking and peering through its lens at things that may or may not still exist. Erevos is patient. It has been consuming matter and bending light for six and a half billion years, and it will continue long after the Observatory's funding expires and its researchers go home. The Whisper will continue whether or not anyone listens. The Lensed Archive will display its distant images whether or not anyone looks. The Maw does not care about its audience. It simply is, and the universe bends around it.
